objectives: Explain what a salary is and how it differs from hourly or freelance pay.
Tell gross pay, deductions and net pay apart on any payslip.
Check a payslip for errors in a fixed order.
Compare two job offers beyond the headline salary.
Ask about a pay rise in specific, workable sentences.
Separate fixed costs from variable costs in a monthly budget.
Name the five habits that quietly cost money every month.

sections.body:
A salary is a regular payment for work, agreed in advance, usually for the same hours and the same job each month. The word covers more than a monthly figure. It also covers the rules that decide how much reaches your bank account.

A salary has four moving parts. The **rate** is what the job is worth: a monthly figure, an hourly figure, or an annual figure divided by the working year. The **contract** says how many hours are expected, how overtime is treated, and what notice period applies if either side wants to end it. The **payslip** is the document that shows what was paid and what was taken off. The **net pay** is what actually arrives in your account.

The distinction that catches people out is between **gross pay** and **net pay**. Gross pay is the amount before anything is deducted. Net pay is what is left after deductions, and it is normally smaller. New employees often compare offers by gross, then discover that two jobs with the same gross leave very different amounts.

Salary also differs from other kinds of pay in one important way: it is paid for the role, not for the hour. A salaried employee usually works a set number of hours, and there is no rule that extra hours are paid extra. Hourly work pays for time, freelance work pays for outcomes or deliverables, and commission pays for results. These are not moral judgements; they are different deals, and they carry different risks.

Understanding the structure is what makes the rest of this article usable. A salary is not one number that appears in your account. It is a rate, a set of deductions, and a difference between what you earn and what you receive.
examples: The offer is 40 $ gross a month, but my net pay is closer to 31 $.
My contract says 40 hours a week and paid overtime after that.
sections.heading: What a salary actually is

sections.body:
Every payslip runs the same route: start with gross pay, subtract the deductions, arrive at net pay.

**Gross pay** is the total for the period before any deductions. It may be a monthly salary, or it may be calculated from hours, a rate, overtime, bonuses and allowances. Read the calculation line, not just the total, because the total can hide a change in hours.

**Deductions** are amounts taken out before you are paid. They usually fall into two groups. **Statutory deductions** are required by law or by the social insurance system, such as income tax, social insurance contributions and retirement contributions. **Other deductions** come from agreements you signed, such as a union membership fee, a staff canteen charge, an advance repayment or a court-ordered amount.

**Net pay** is what remains, and it is the number that reaches your bank account. The line called net pay, take-home pay or transferred is the one to compare against your budget.

Tax in most systems is **withheld** rather than paid directly. The employer calculates what you owe on the money you earned this period, takes it out, and reports it. That is why a payslip tax figure is not your final tax bill, and why a large refund or a demand at the end of the year can both happen.

Three checks are worth making on every payslip. Does gross pay match your agreed rate and hours? Have all the deductions you expect actually appeared? Does net pay match the payment that reached your account? Any mismatch is worth raising while the period is still recent, because employers can usually correct an error quickly and much less easily two years later.
examples: The gross is 40 $, and after tax and insurance my net pay is 31 $.
This line is the tax withheld for the month, not my final tax bill.
The hours on the payslip are not the hours I actually worked.
sections.heading: Gross pay, deductions and net pay

sections.body:
A payslip is short, dense and identical from month to month, so it is easy to stop reading it. Five minutes in a fixed order turns it into a document you can use.

The order matters. Start with the header: who the employer is, which period the slip covers, and your own identity number. A payslip for the wrong period or the wrong person is the most common clerical error, and it is easiest to catch at the top.

Then work from the top of the arithmetic downwards, and check the arithmetic yourself. Gross, minus deductions, equals net. If the slip does not add up, nothing below it can be trusted.

Finally compare with the last slip and with your bank account. A payslip that is correct on its own can still be wrong in context, because a missing overtime line or a wrong bonus will not look wrong in isolation.
examples: The slip covers a different month, so I am asking for the right one.
The overtime line is missing from this month's slip.
The net pay on the slip is 5 $ more than what arrived in my account.
sections.heading: How to read a payslip in the right order
steps: Check the header: employer, pay period, your identity number.
Find the gross pay figure and the calculation behind it.
List every deduction line and check each one against what you expect.
Check that gross minus deductions equals net pay.
Compare the net pay with the amount that reached your account.
Compare this slip with last month's and note anything that changed.

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet on the payslip, in the contract and in the conversation with your employer.

**Gross pay** is the pay before deductions. **Net pay** is what is left after them and paid to you. **Deduction** is any amount subtracted from gross pay. **Tax withheld** is the income tax taken out in advance by the employer.

**Social insurance** is the compulsory contributory scheme that covers sickness, maternity, accidents and retirement. **Pension contribution** is the part of your pay set aside for your own retirement, matched in many systems by the employer.

**Allowance** is a payment on top of the salary for a specific reason: transport, meals, housing, or a phone. It may be taxable and it may be worth more than it looks, because it is often paid without deductions.

**Overtime** is work beyond the agreed hours, usually paid at a higher rate. **Bonus** is a payment that is not part of the base salary and usually depends on results or on company performance.

**Probation period** is the first months of a new job, often with a shorter notice period and a shorter period for an employer to end the contract. **Notice period** is the time you must give, or must be given, before the contract ends.

**Annual leave** is paid time off, usually counted in days and often accruing monthly. **Expense** is money the company owes you back for work you paid for yourself, and it usually needs a receipt.
sections.heading: The words on a payslip and in a contract

terms.example: My gross pay is 40 $ a month, before anything is taken off.
terms.gloss: Total pay for the period before any money is deducted for tax, insurance or other agreed deductions.

terms.example: The difference between my gross and my net is mostly tax and insurance.
terms.gloss: The amount left after all deductions, and the amount that reaches your bank account.

terms.example: The canteen charge is a deduction, so it comes out before my net pay.
terms.gloss: Any amount taken off gross pay before payment, whether required by law or agreed with you.

terms.example: The tax withheld this month was higher because my bonus was large.
terms.gloss: Income tax taken out of your pay in advance by the employer. It is not your final tax bill.

terms.example: My social insurance contribution is a percentage of my gross pay.
terms.gloss: The compulsory payment into the social insurance system that covers sickness, maternity, accidents and retirement.

terms.example: I submitted the taxi receipts as an expense claim on Friday.
terms.gloss: Money you paid for work that the company owes you back. It almost always needs a receipt and a deadline.

sections.body:
A pay conversation goes badly when it is a request without evidence. It goes well when it is a short presentation of what you do, what it is worth, and what you want.

Prepare three things. Your **record**: what you delivered this year, in numbers where you can get them. Your **market position**: what the same role pays elsewhere, and what people at your level earn. Your **ask**: one number, and the date you want it to start.

Choose the moment. A review meeting, a promotion, or a job you have just finished are all better than a quiet Tuesday. If there is no scheduled review, ask for one: "Could we schedule thirty minutes to talk about my salary and my development?" is a normal thing to say.

When you speak, describe your value before your need. "I have taken over the two largest accounts and raised revenue by 12 %" lands better than "I need more money", because the first gives the manager something to take to their own boss.

Then make the ask specific. "I would like my salary reviewed to 45 $ a month from the 1st of next month" is a request that can be answered. "I would like to discuss my compensation" is not, and it usually ends without an answer at all.

If the answer is no, keep it professional and ask two questions: what would need to change for a review, and when can we talk again. Then put the date in your calendar and keep producing the record you would need for it. Most pay rises that eventually happen were requested more than once.
examples: I have run the two largest accounts since March, and revenue on them is up 12 %.
I would like my salary reviewed to 45 $ a month from the 1st of next month.
Could we schedule thirty minutes to talk about my salary and my development?
What would need to change for a review, and when can we talk again?
sections.heading: Asking about a pay rise, and what to say

sections.body:
The headline salary is the easiest number to compare and the least useful one. Two offers with the same gross can leave very different amounts in your account, and they can cost you very different amounts of money as well.

Compare **net pay** first, then the **contract terms**. A higher gross with heavier deductions can leave you worse off. And the gross number on an offer letter may quietly include an allowance that is taxed differently, or a bonus that only appears in a good year.

Then look at the **annual total**, which is gross multiplied by the number of months paid, including the thirteenth-month payment, bonuses and allowances if they are written into the contract. Take a full year of income, not a month, because annual costs like insurance and travel differ as much as salary does.

Next, price the **working time**. A higher salary with fifty extra unpaid hours a week is not a higher salary; it is a lower hourly rate with extra pressure. Divide the annual income by the realistic hours you will work, including commuting and unpaid preparation.

Then price the **benefits**: health cover, retirement matching, leave, training, a phone, a transport allowance. These are real money, and they are worth more than the same amount in salary if you would have bought them yourself.

And price the **risk**. A small company pays more but may not exist next year. A freelancer invoice may not be paid for ninety days. A generous offer with a six-month probation and one month's notice can end much faster than it looks.

Write the two offers on one page, in the same order, with the same headings. Differences that matter become obvious on paper and disappear in conversation.
examples: Offer A pays 5 $ more gross, but my net would be lower after deductions.
Counting the annual bonus, the second offer is actually 1200 $ a year better.
The first job pays more per hour, but not once I count the extra hours.
sections.heading: Comparing two job offers without fooling yourself

sections.body:
A budget is not a restriction. It is a plan for the month before the month arrives, and it works only if it is built from your real numbers rather than an ideal version of you.

Start with the **fixed costs**: rent, utilities, insurance, transport, subscriptions, loan repayments. These are the same every month, and they are the floor your income has to clear. If your fixed costs are 70 % of your net pay, you have 30 % left for everything else, and you should know that number before anything else.

Then the **variable costs**: food, household goods, clothes, going out. These move, and they are where a good month hides a bad month. Track them for one month without changing anything, because most people do not know their real figures.

Then the **goals**: savings, an emergency fund, a course, a trip, a deposit. These are not what is left over at the end; they are set aside on the day the salary arrives.

A simple split helps: a common rule is 50 % for needs, 30 % for wants and 20 % for savings and debt. Treat it as a starting point, not a law. A student with a small income and a large loan needs a different split from a household with two salaries.

Build it as **pay yourself first**. On the day the salary lands, move the savings amount to a separate account before you start spending. What remains is what you actually live on for the month, and it is usually more than you expected.

Review the budget every month, on the same date, for ten minutes. Look for the leaks rather than the totals: three small subscriptions nobody uses cost less attention than one habit you keep rewriting, and both are worth the same ten minutes.
examples: My fixed costs are 70 % of my net pay, so I know what I really have to live on.
I move the savings out on payday, so the rest is what I spend.
I cancelled two subscriptions I had forgotten about, and that is 19 $ a month back.
sections.heading: Where the money goes: building a budget you keep

sections.body:
**Paying the minimum on a card** keeps a balance alive at a rate that dwarfs every other habit on this list.

**Letting a small balance sit** on a store card or an overdraft facility is the same mistake in a smaller costume, and the fees are designed to be small enough to ignore.

**Subscriptions you never cancel** are the most common quiet leak. One per month at a modest price is a yearly amount that never appears in your accounts.

**Paying late** is priced as an inconvenience. It is actually a fee on top of a penalty rate, and often a mark against your credit history, which is what decides what you are offered next time.

**Borrowing to cover a habit** rather than to cover an emergency turns a temporary gap into a total number with an interest rate attached.
sections.heading: Five habits that quietly cost money

sections.body:
Money conversations at work are uncomfortable mostly because people avoid the numbers. These sentences fix that by naming a figure, so nobody has to guess what you mean.

Use them in three situations: when you are offered a role, when a payslip looks wrong, and when you need a payment to happen on a particular date. In all three, the number and the date are what make the sentence workable.

Keep the tone level. A question with a figure in it is a professional question, not a complaint, and it is much harder to dismiss than an impression.
examples: Could you confirm the net pay for this contract, after deductions?
The overtime on this payslip is not the 6 hours I worked. Could you check it?
Could this invoice be paid by the 25th, so I can schedule the payment?
I would like to understand how the allowance is treated for tax.
Is there a review scheduled for this year, and what would we discuss?
I would like to claim these receipts. What is the deadline and the process?
sections.heading: Sentences you can use about money at work

item.summary: Money at work has its own language, and most people learn it by accident. After reading this you can read a payslip, tell gross pay from net pay, compare two job offers properly, ask for a raise without guessing, and build a budget you can keep.
